newsitem.title: USA: Fund flows strong in January.
newsitem.headline: Fund flows strong in January.

text.p: The amount of cash Americans ploughed into mutual funds doubled in January from December, an industry group said Wednesday, and the level of investment was expected to be strong, though not quite as strong, this month.
"The small investor's love affair with stock funds continues unabated," said Laurence Dwyer, a spokesman for New England Investment Cos., a mutual fund investment firm.
Analysts said the stock market's strong showing in January drew in even more investors.
"The market has done very well and that's attracted money," said Charles Biderman, president of Mutual Fund Trim Tabs, which tracks fund activity.
The amount of cash flow into U.S. stock mutual funds rose to $24 billion in January from $12.2 billion in December, the Investment Company Institute, an industry group, said Wednesday.
While the performance was strong, it fell short of the record of $28.9 billion in new cash invested in January 1996.
Vanguard Group recorded total inflows of $4.9 billion in January, a record, with about $3.4 billion going into stock funds, Vanguard spokesman Brian Mattes said.
"It appears that February is going to be on target to rival January, but it probably won't beat January," he said.
The most popular funds so far this month have been large blue-chip funds, index funds, and growth and income funds, he said.
Tax-free bond funds also showed strength, due in part to the upcoming April 15 deadlines for tax returns. In January, inflows into tax-free bond funds were five times the December rate.
Mattes traced the strong overall flows to a "very strong stock market right out of the of box in January. Investors tend to want to invest when the market is going up."
The Dow Jones industrial average rose nearly 6 percent in January and the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks performed even better, rising 6.1 percent.
Charles Schwab Corp. said net new cash flow into stock funds totalled about $430 million through Feb. 11, vs. $653 million in the comparable period in January.
So far this month, the strongest sectors were domestic growth funds and international growth funds, spokesman Glen Mathison said.
New England Investment had a record January and "it looks like another strong month in February," said Dwyer.
T. Rowe Price Associates Inc. also set a cash flow record in January, although it also declined to provide details. The company recorded total inflows of $1.6 billion in January 1996.
Analysts do not expect the flow of cash into mutual funds to end in case of a market "correction" where stocks fall 5 percent to 10 percent.

"Even if we see market volatility, the underlying commitment to stock and fund investments is very strong and a price decline is not going to be enough to break that commitment," said Avi Nachmany, head of research at Strategic Insight, a fund research firm.
